# Nimijātaka (Ja 541)

**ID:** Ja 541
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Nimijātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Good King Nimi
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja541
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nimijātaka* (Ja 541; PTS J vi 95–129), found among the final great stories of the *Jātaka* collection, is framed as a teaching delivered by the Buddha while walking in Makhādeva's mango park near Mithilā, prompted by a smile when he recalls dwelling there in a former life [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2014; Human Nature and Conflict]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta is King Nimi of Mithilā, an exemplary monarch who guides his subjects in morality and generous giving [Appleton 2014; Human Nature and Conflict]. Because of this righteous governance, his former citizens are reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa), where they ask Sakka (Indra) to invite their king to visit heaven [Appleton 2014; Braarvig 2009]. Sakka sends his charioteer Mātali (identified with Ānanda) to fetch Nimi; Mātali conducts the king on a vivid tour of the hell realms—explaining the specific karmic causes of the punishments—before escorting him to the celestial mansions [Appleton 2014; Braarvig 2009]. During this cosmic journey, they pass the seven concentric mountains around Mount Meru across the subtle waters of the ocean Sīdā [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 1988]. Like King Makhādeva before him, Nimi subsequently abdicates in favor of his son upon noticing his first grey hair, renouncing worldly rule for the ascetic life [Human Nature and Conflict; Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014].

Nimi's infernal tour served as a foundational template for Buddhist descriptions of hell, influencing subsequent works such as the northern Thai *Māleyyatherasutta* and the cosmology of the *Trai Phum Phra Ruang* [Braarvig 2009; Cousins et al. 1974; Jory 2016]. The narrative shares its central abdication motif with the *Makhādeva Sutta* (MN 83), the *Makhādevajātaka* (Ja 9), and parallels in the Chinese Āgamas (MĀ 67, EĀ 50.4, T 152.87, and T 211.38) [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus both document extensive textual reuse and parallels between the *Nimijātaka* and other Pali works, notably the *Sādhinajātaka* (Ja 494), *Revatīvimānavatthu* (Vv 52), *Revatīpetavatthu* (Pv 39), *Catumahārājasutta* (AN 3.37–38), *Sānusutta* (SN 10.5), and multiple narratives in the *Vimānavatthu* (Vv 22–25, 37) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the text with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and Chinese Āgama collections [DharmaNexus].

- [Cousins et al. 1974] L. Cousins, A. Kunst, and K. R. Norman, eds., Buddhist Studies in Honour of I.B. Horner (1974) — Notes the influence of the Nimijātaka hell visit on the apocryphal northern Thai Māleyyatherasutta.

- [Human Nature and Conflict] Human Nature and Conflict: A Buddhist Perspective — Cites Ja 541 (J. vi. 95–129) regarding Nimi's abdication in favour of his son upon seeing his first grey hair.
- [Jory 2016] Patrick Jory, Thailand’s Theory of Monarchy: Vessantara Jātaka and the Idea of the Perfect Man (2016) — Mentions King Nimi's hell journey in the Thai cosmological treatise Trai Phum Phra Ruang.
